meta.title: A brick house split on a stud lattice and built in bricks
meta.description: A SHORT TERRACE OF HOUSES DERIVED BY A SPLIT GRAMMAR ON AN INTEGER LATTICE, THEN BUILT IN BRICKS. Every terminal of the grammar is an axis-aligned box whose corners are WHOLE NUMBERS -- x and z in studs, y in plates, a plate 0.4 of a stud -- carrying a string `kind` (wall, glass, door, trim, roof, floor, ground, chimney) and a palette colour; `packBricks` turns those boxes into catalogue bricks, and the house is drawn as three instance batches: bricks, the studs left showing, and the pots on its chimneys. THE GRAMMAR IS TWO RULE TABLES, each an `applyRules`. A rule is a pin pair in the wrapper's body named after the label it rewrites, the label is `kind`, and a label no rule claims is TERMINAL -- so a piece's label is the material it is built in, and nothing relabels it into a kind afterwards. MASSING runs from the lot: `block` (cut in two along its longer floor axis while both halves keep `minBlock` studs, three rounds deep, the third only for a block still longer than 16 studs; a block not cut becomes a `mass`), `mass` (draws the block's storeys, colours, door wall, setback and trim, then cuts the air over its footprint into its ground slab, its lower tier and the rest, `upper`), `upper` (steps in by the setback and cuts into the upper tier and the roof space over the top tier), `roofSpace` (a declared draw: flat, else hip, else gable), and one rule for each roof style. FACADE runs from the tiers: `tier` (cut into storeys, each broken into its shell), `face` (a wall cut into bays), `bay` (a declared draw: an opening, or wall), `opening` (the pieces round a window or a door) and `sill`. Each rule is a chain of one to eight nodes, most of them two or three, and reading the body top to bottom is reading the grammar. Every rule application costs a round, and the wrapper's `ruleDepth` is the round, which is how the block rule keeps to three rounds of cutting. THE GRAMMAR CUTS. `splitBox` cuts a box along one axis into labelled pieces -- `absolute` lengths, `relative` shares of the rest, or a `repeat` of equal pieces about one module long -- every attribute riding onto every piece, and its sizes are a field resolved on the PARENT, so a decision both halves share is made once: a block's cut, `clamp(floor(span * (0.35 + 0.3 * ruleRoll) + 0.5), minBlock, span - minBlock)` studs from its min side, puts both halves on one integer coordinate. A label of `""` is a GAP that takes its space and emits nothing, which is how a setback steps in (a gap on each lot-edge side of the upper tier) and how each layer of a pitched roof steps in (a gap of `layer` studs either side). A piece of no size is DROPPED, which is how one opening rule serves every opening: a door's sill and the wall under it, the sill of a block that rolled none, and a lintel that rolled none come out with no height and are not emitted, with no branch. Because a cut can only divide what is there, the lot is a column of AIR as tall as any house can stand, and a mass's storeys and roof are cut from it, the air over the roof a gap. THE PER-BLOCK DECISIONS are made in the `mass` rule, on the block, before it is cut, so every piece of it carries them: `storeys`, `wallTint`, `roofTint`, `doorWall`, `inset`, `lowSt` and `trim` (the sill and lintel rolls, and the house's plinth roll). The roof style is a DECLARED DRAW: the `roofSpace` rule is a string `setAttribute` whose `values` are gable, hip and flat and whose index is `select(lt(ruleRoll, flatRoofRate), 2, lt(ruleRoll, flatRoofRate + (1 - flatRoofRate) * hipRoofRate))`, one roll against both rates; the bay rule's opening-or-wall is the same shape, on `windowRate`. `ruleRoll` is the wrapper's own roll for each rule application. TIERS AND STOREYS. A mass is its ground slab, then the lower tier, then the upper part. A tier is a whole number of storeys, each `storeyHeight` plates: `shellSplit` breaks a storey into the CEILING slab over it, a plate over the full footprint that is the next storey's floor (or the tier's ceiling over the top storey), and the four walls under it, south and north full length and west and east between them. A SETBACK (`setbackRate`) steps a block of two storeys or more in above a storey drawn from the first to the one under the top, by `inset` studs on every side the block has on the lot edge (two where that keeps four studs a side, else one, else none and no setback), a party wall staying flush with its neighbour; the upper tier stands on the lower tier's top ceiling, which is its first floor and the terrace round it in one slab, held by the walls below and the walls above alike. Only the top tier is roofed: the roof space is cut from the upper part over the upper tier, or over the whole mass when there is no setback. ROOFS. A GABLE's layers step in one stud on the two long sides, its ridge along the long axis and the stud at each end of a layer its gable wall, in the wall's colour; a HIP's layers step in one stud on all four sides, so it closes to a ridge as long as the long side less the short, and two studs more (one for an odd short side); both rise `roofStep` plates a layer for `ceil(short / 2)` layers, cut from the roof space as a `repeat` of `roofStep` with the air over them a gap, each layer told its index in `layer`. A FLAT roof is the top tier's ceiling slab with a parapet on its edge, one stud thick and three plates tall, over the walls below: a `shellSplit` of the four walls alone. The ceiling under every roof is what lets a roof stand on a floor rather than over an empty attic. THE WALLS CARRY THEIR OWN FRAME. `shellSplit` writes on every wall the axis it runs along and the sign that makes it run LEFT TO RIGHT AS SEEN FROM OUTSIDE (`alongAxis`, `alongSign`), its outward normal (`outward`) and its face code (`face`: 1 south, 2 north, 3 west, 4 east), so the facade rules are written ONCE for every wall: the bay split is `splitBox` with axis `perCell` on `alongAxis` and `direction` `alongSign`, `max(1, floor(len / bayWidth))` bays snapped to whole studs, slot 0 the leftmost seen from outside; the opening is set in its bay from the left, as nearly centred as whole studs allow, `openingWidth` studs at most with a stud of jamb either side; and a sill stands out by adding `outward` to its box. The DOOR goes on the ground floor -- the storey whose walls start on the slab over the baseplate, `box("y0")` = 2 -- of the first lot-edge wall, south, then north, else west, else east, in the middle bay. Every block has such a wall: a cut along one axis never moves a block off the lot edges of the other, so a block with neither a south nor a north edge was cut along z on both sides, which takes two of the three rounds, and the one left cannot cut it off both the west and the east edge; with `minBlock` at least 5 that side wall is three studs or more between the south and north walls, wide enough for a door bay. BOX NAMES. A field reads the box of the cell it is evaluated on by name -- `box("x0")`, `box("sz")`, `box("center")`, `box("lo")` and the rest -- so a size, an axis or a margin is written in the cell's own terms with nothing carried aside, and a split's sizes read the PARENT's box. A `let` names a value one field reads more than once (a wall's length, the opening it takes); like a box name, it is notation for the field written out. A WINDOW GOES ONLY WHERE A WALL IS EXPOSED, and exposure is a query, not an assumption. Blocks share party walls, and a tall block beside a low one has a wall that is covered at the bottom and open above. The `bay` rule asks `boxContact` whether a PROBE overlaps anything the massing made -- every slab, tier and roof piece, and every chimney's shadow (below), merged and fed to the facade stage as a BROADCAST input. The probe is the bay's own box carved by the node's `marginMin` and `marginMax`, fields of the bay's box names and frame: along the wall the opening's width less a quarter stud at each end, so it crosses every stud of the opening and no stud beside it; up the wall the one course where the opening starts -- for a window with a sill, the sill's course, the cells the sill stands out into; through the wall a sheet half a stud OUTSIDE its face. Bottom is enough because everything the massing makes stacks on the ground with nothing overhanging, so if the bottom of the opening is free, every course above it is. This is why the grammar is two stages: a query reads an EARLIER stage, never the frontier still being rewritten. A CHIMNEY (`chimneyRate`) is a stack one stud by two, its long side along the ridge, rising four plates past the top of its roof, with a pot on each of its two top studs. It is PLACED rather than cut -- it stands in the air beside the upper layers of a roof, a box no split of the roof space makes -- so it is read from the massing's `trail`, the cells each rule rewrote: every roof space the style rule took, its box the top tier's footprint from the tier's top up, is rolled, and one `setBounds` places the stack. On a pitched roof it stands on the exposed one-stud step of a layer in the upper half below the top, front or back by a roll: every layer above that one starts a stud further in, so the stack stands on the roof and overlaps no piece, and along the ridge it keeps off a gable's end studs. On a flat roof it stands on the parapet's long side, over the wall below, which holds it. For the window query a chimney counts as its SHADOW: the stack grown two studs every way across the roof, kept inside its tier, from the tier's top up past its pots, because a stack standing a stud or two off a taller neighbour's wall is still in front of that wall's windows, past the probe half a stud out. The pots are found rather than placed: a pot goes on every showing stud of a chimney brick with nothing resting on it, so in a partial build it comes with the chimney's last course. THE FACADE TRIM is what keeps a big wall from reading flat up close: sills, lintels, a plinth, and bricks that are not all one colour. A SILL (`sillRate`) is a plate under a window, as wide as it, its top at `sillHeight`, standing one stud out from the wall face: a plate two studs deep, one row in the wall standing on the wall under it and one outside, held through the wall. Its outer studs are not drawn -- a stud on a trim brick that nothing ever rests on is dropped from the studs batch -- so it reads as a smooth ledge. A LINTEL (`lintelRate`) is a block over each window and door, as wide as the opening and a brick tall, less where the wall over the opening is shorter. Both are the opening's width, not wider: a bay keeps a stud of jamb either side, often only one, and trim a stud wider met the next window's and ran along the wall as a band. Sill and lintel are kind `trim`, in the TRIM colour: on a wall with a hue its colour darkened, and on a white or grey wall a warm sandstone, because a neutral trim on the pale glass reads as more of the pane. A PLINTH (`plinthRate`) lays every wall brick standing on the ground floor's slab in dark grey. Sills and lintels are rolled ONCE PER BLOCK, so every window of a block agrees; the plinth ONCE PER HOUSE, because it is laid on the packed bricks and a brick can run on across two blocks' walls of one colour. And `brickVariation` is the share of wall bricks laid in an OFF-SHADE of their wall's colour, half darker and half lighter. The plinth and the off-shades are coloured on the BRICKS, after the packing, each brick drawing on its own identity, so neither moves a joint; a stud takes the tint of the brick it stands on, gathered by `transferByIndex` through the `brickId` packBricks wrote on it. THE BUILD. `packBricks` reads the pieces' world corners -- the last `setBounds` converts the lattice to world units and centres the lot -- keeps `kind` and colour apart with `groupBy`, and lays every wall in full bricks with the joints staggered course to course; the catalogue is the default one with the BASEPLATES appended through `extraBricks` -- every size of 16, 24, 32 and 40 studs a side, either way round -- and the ground is exactly one of them, one piece under the whole lot: on each axis the lot plus two studs either side, rounded up to a multiple of eight. A floor slab runs on across every block of its storey (the slabs share a kind and a colour), and neighbouring blocks each build their own wall, so a party wall is two studs thick. THE MESHES ARE THE GRAPH'S OWN: three outputs carry `role: "asset"`, so `brick` (a unit box), `stud` (a twelve-sided `meshPrimitive` cylinder, capped on top and open underneath) and `pot` are the meshes the three spawners' asset ids resolve to. One box serves every brick because a brick point's `scale` is its own-frame size and its `rot` the quarter turn of a brick laid sideways; a hairline gap is taken off every `scale` so the joints read, and the stud and pot meshes stand half that gap low so they sit on the brick as drawn. WHAT HOLDS TOGETHER is measured, not assumed. `brickConnectivity` numbers the pieces stud clutch alone holds together and gives every brick a build STEP: courses bottom up, a brick placed when it stands on the baseplate or grips one already placed, a plate hung under a floor placed with the floor. An upper storey's slab is ONE plate between empty rooms with walls only at its edges, so each of its plates has to reach a wall by itself; the packer answers it with plates up to 2x16, a `bond` reward for joining pieces, a charge for every loose plate a placement commits the build to, weighed before the score, and a HOLD SEARCH that lifts a course with a loose plate and solves the slab exactly, bounded in steps rather than time so every machine gets the same house. The grammar answers the rest: a house has a ceiling under its roof; a third split round cuts a block still longer than 16 studs, because a one-plate slab that size, an upper floor or a flat roof, was past what the hold search always solves within its budget; a flat roof is the ceiling itself with only the parapet on it; a setback's upper tier starts on the lower tier's ceiling plate rather than on a slab of its own; and a chimney on a flat roof stands on the parapet, over the wall. A brick no order could attach would get step -1, which says so: the whole build draws it, and every partial build leaves it out rather than show it hanging in air. THE `buildStep` PARAM shows the build as it stands after that step: bricks are kept while their step is at most it, and a stud shows once its brick is placed and until the brick resting on it is. The packer is asked for EVERY stud (`studMode: all`), and the studs go through `brickConnectivity` alongside the bricks, which writes on each stud the step of both. The param's maximum, 138, is an upper bound on how tall a house can stand, in plates, taken from every param below at the top of its range -- the ceiling over the most storeys at the tallest storey, the taller of a pitched roof and a parapet, and a chimney's rise -- and so it is the whole build for every house; the exact range for one house is the `stepCount` detail `brickConnectivity` writes. It is also the height of the lot's air column. THE OTHER PARAMS are the grammar's own numbers, each READ by name with `param("...")` in the field slots that use it -- the two rule stages declare the ones their bodies read and are fed the graph's own -- so at its default every one cooks exactly what the literal it replaced did: `storeyHeight`, `sillHeight` and `headHeight` in plates, `bayWidth`, `openingWidth` and `minBlock` in studs, `windowRate`, `minStoreys` and `maxStoreys`, `roofStep`, the four rates of the roofs, chimneys and setbacks and the four of the facade trim, and the lot's range, `lotWidthMin`/`lotWidthMax` and `lotDepthMin`/`lotDepthMax`. A value that must land on the lattice is rounded where it is read, `floor(param("storeyHeight") + 0.5)`, and a lot side is rounded down to an even number so the lot centres on whole studs; a max below its min reads as the min. The ranges hold jointly: every sill is below every head, and every head two plates under the lowest storey, so no combination makes an opening or a lintel of no height. Some numbers stay literals by choice -- the palette, the trim's shade and sandstone, the off-shades' two factors, a sill's one stud out and a lintel's brick of height, the cut's 0.35 + 0.3 spread, the probe's half stud, the parapet's three plates, a chimney's footprint, rise and shadow, the setback's inset, the baseplate's margin -- and some because no field reaches their slot: the lattice pitch, the baseplate sizes (`extraBricks`) and the stud and pot meshes, and so the brick gap. THE LOT STOPS AT 32 x 32, which stands on the largest baseplate, 40 x 40, with four studs of it showing on every side. Measured on this grammar, not assumed from the one before it: the first 2000 seeds at the default params came out in one piece, with no brick step -1 and no piece claiming a lattice cell of another material, and so did 200 seeds with every param at its maximum and 200 at its minimum, 150 on a 32 x 32 lot of four storeys, 200 on that lot under each roof style forced, and 300 each with the trim, chimneys and setbacks forced on, with them forced off and every bay a window, on an 8 x 8 lot of four storeys with chimneys and setbacks forced, and with the lowest sill under the highest head in the shortest storey.

params.name: buildStep
params.description: Show the build as it stands after this many steps, counting from 0. A step is one course of the build placed bottom up, with anything hanging under a brick placed alongside it; the default and maximum, 138, is an upper bound on how tall a house can stand in plates, taken from every other param at the top of its range, so it is past every house's last step and shows the whole build -- including any brick no order can attach (step -1), which every smaller value hides rather than draw hanging in air. The exact range for one house is the stepCount detail brickConnectivity writes: steps 0 to stepCount - 1.

params.name: storeyHeight
params.description: Plates from one storey's floor to the next, its one-plate floor slab included: 16 is the slab and five bricks of wall. Rounded to a whole plate.

params.name: sillHeight
params.description: Plates from a storey's floor up to the bottom of every window, which is the top of its sill where it has one. Rounded to a whole plate; its range ends below headHeight's, so a window always has a height.

params.name: headHeight
params.description: Plates from a storey's floor up to the top of every window and door. Rounded to a whole plate; its range ends two plates under the lowest storeyHeight, so a wall keeps at least one plate over its openings, the plate a lintel takes first.

params.name: bayWidth
params.description: Target bay width in studs: a wall L studs long takes max(1, floor(L / bayWidth)) bays, cut on whole studs, and each bay holds at most one window or door.

params.name: openingWidth
params.description: Widest window or door, in studs, rounded to a whole stud; a bay keeps at least a stud of wall either side, so a narrower bay takes a narrower opening.

params.name: windowRate
params.description: Chance that a bay wide enough for an opening, and exposed, takes a window rather than staying solid wall. Doors do not roll.

params.name: sillRate
params.description: Chance that a block's windows have SILLS: under each window a plate as wide as the window, its top at sillHeight, standing one stud out from the wall face, in the block's trim colour (its wall colour darkened, or a warm sandstone on a white or grey wall). The studs on its outer row are not drawn, so it reads as a smooth ledge. A window with a sill opens only where the cells the sill stands out into are clear as well. Doors have none. Rolled per block, so every window of a block agrees.

params.name: lintelRate
params.description: Chance that a block's windows and doors have LINTELS: over each opening a block of the trim colour as wide as the opening and a brick tall, less where the wall over the opening is shorter. Rolled per block.

params.name: plinthRate
params.description: Chance that the house stands on a PLINTH: every wall brick whose bottom is the ground floor's bottom course, round every block, laid in dark grey. Rolled once for the whole house, not per block: it is laid on the packed bricks, and a brick can run on across the walls of two blocks of one colour, so a roll per block would spill into a neighbour that had none.

params.name: brickVariation
params.description: Share of wall bricks laid in an OFF-SHADE of their wall's colour, drawn brick by brick: half of them darker (0.88 of the colour), half lighter (1.1 of it, each channel capped at 1). Applied to the packed bricks, so it never moves a joint, and a brick's studs take its shade. 0 lays every wall in one colour.

params.name: minBlock
params.description: Smallest side, in studs, a split may leave: a block is cut in two only when both halves are at least this wide, in each of three rounds (the third only cuts a block longer than 16 studs). Rounded to a whole stud. It starts at 5 so that a block with no south or north lot edge, whose door goes on a side wall between them, has a wall at least three studs long for it.

params.name: minStoreys
params.description: Fewest storeys a block draws. Rounded; a maxStoreys below it reads as this.

params.name: maxStoreys
params.description: Most storeys a block draws: each block takes a whole number uniformly from minStoreys to this.

params.name: roofStep
params.description: Plates each layer of a pitched roof rises while it steps in one stud: on both long sides for a gable, on all four for a hip. Rounded to a whole plate.

params.name: flatRoofRate
params.description: Chance that a block's roof is flat: its ceiling slab, grey like every floor, with a parapet on the edge one stud thick and three plates tall, the parapet in the roof's colour. Drawn first; a block that does not take it has a pitched roof.

params.name: hipRoofRate
params.description: Chance that a pitched roof is a hip, stepping in on all four sides, rather than a gable, stepping in on the two long sides between gable ends. 0 makes every pitched roof a gable.

params.name: chimneyRate
params.description: Chance that a block's roof has a chimney: a stack one stud by two rising from a roof step (from the parapet on a flat roof) four plates past the roof's top, with a pot on each of its two top studs.

params.name: setbackRate
params.description: Chance that a block of two storeys or more steps its upper storeys in from the storeys below, on the sides it has on the lot edge, leaving a terrace; the roof stands on the upper storeys. A block with no lot-edge side, or too small to step in and keep four studs a side, never does.

params.name: lotWidthMin
params.description: Narrowest lot, along x, in studs, rounded down to an even number so the lot centres on whole studs. The baseplate grows with the lot, keeping at least two studs of it on every side.

params.name: lotWidthMax
params.description: Widest lot, along x, in studs: the width is drawn in even steps from lotWidthMin to this, and a value below the min reads as the min.

params.name: lotDepthMin
params.description: Shallowest lot, along z, in studs, rounded down to an even number.

params.name: lotDepthMax
params.description: Deepest lot, along z, in studs: the depth is drawn in even steps from lotDepthMin to this, and a value below the min reads as the min.

params.name: storeyHeight
params.description: The graph param storeyHeight, read by name in the rules.
